title: The clever steward (Luke 16:1–13)
hook: a crooked manager is praised for being shrewd; you can't serve God and mammon

segments.voice: Yesterday, a builder sat down to count before he built his tower. Your line was sit down and reckon. What did you count? Day four hundred seventy-one.

This is a parable preachers sometimes approach carefully, and readers still argue about parts of it. A manager is caught wasting his boss's money. He's about to be fired. So he spends his last afternoon cooking the books in his customers' favor. And at the end of the story, the boss praises him. It sounds like Jesus is applauding fraud. He isn't. But to see what he is doing, you have to watch the manager's hands. Today, the clever steward.
screen: `A PARABLE READERS STILL ARGUE ABOUT.` → `CAUGHT WASTING THE BOSS'S MONEY.` → `AND THE BOSS PRAISES HIM.`

segments.voice: A rich man hears his steward has wasted his goods. He calls him in: give an account, you're done. The steward thinks fast. I can't dig, I'm ashamed to beg. I know what I'll do, so that people will take me into their homes. He calls in his master's debtors one by one. How much do you owe? A hundred barrels of oil. Sit down quickly, write fifty. And you? A hundred quarters of wheat. Write eighty. He's making friends with the only currency he has left. Then the surprising line: "And the lord commended the unjust steward, forasmuch as he had done wisely: for the children of this world are wiser in their generation than the children of light." Notice what's praised. Not the dishonesty. He's still called unjust. What's praised is that he saw the end coming and acted. He knew his position wouldn't last, and he used what was passing through his hands to make friends who would last. Jesus draws the lesson: make friends with the mammon of iniquity, so that when you fail, when your own time runs out, they may receive you into everlasting dwellings. Mammon is the Douay's word for wealth, money and property. In the Catholic reading, everyone is a steward like this one, who will one day be asked to give an account. So the parable says: use it now, while it's in your hands, for people. Then the line the passage ends on: "You cannot serve God and mammon." No servant can serve two masters. The steward was crooked, but he understood one thing perfectly: what you hold, you won't hold forever.
screen: `GIVE AN ACCOUNT. YOU'RE DONE.` · `A HUNDRED BARRELS? WRITE FIFTY.` · `PRAISED FOR SEEING THE END COMING.` · `WHEN YOU FAIL, FRIENDS RECEIVE YOU.` · then, large: `YOU CANNOT SERVE GOD AND MAMMON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: use money for friendship. Settle, and breathe. Picture what's passing through your hands this week: a paycheck, an allowance, a budget, even a few dollars. None of it stays. Now think of one person you could do something good for with a small part of it. Buy a coworker lunch. Pay for a friend's coffee. Send something to a family that's struggling. Pick one, and decide when. If you pray, ask to be a faithful steward. The bell holds the time.
The clever steward. A crooked manager praised not for cheating but for seeing the end coming and using money to make friends. Today's word.
Your line: god or mammon. Today, spend one small amount of money on purpose for someone else's good, and notice which master you're serving. Day four hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Catholics often speak of stewardship, the idea that time, talent and money are entrusted by God rather than owned outright, and some parishes ask members to make an annual stewardship commitment.

fork.setup: you're the steward. you're fired, and you have one afternoon left with the books. what do you do?
options: beg the master for one more chance.
call in the debtors and cut their bills.
quietly take some money for yourself.
fork.reveal: he cuts their debts so they'll welcome him later. the master commends him for acting wisely, though he's still called unjust.

original.note: Greek, from Aramaic mamona: wealth, property, what a person trusts in.

trapdoor: what you thought: this parable says a little fraud is fine if it's clever.
what it means: the steward is still unjust; he's praised for seeing his time is short and using money to make lasting friends.
what a scholar hears: in verse 8 Luke calls the master kyrios, the same word he uses for Jesus, which is part of why readers still argue over who does the praising.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): removed the narrator's 'every one of us is a steward' (now 'in the Catholic reading'); Luke 16:9 paraphrase corrected to the Douay's 'when you shall fail' (the voice had followed the 'when it fails' reading); 'measures' changed to the Douay's 'quarters' of wheat; cut 'the line everyone remembers' and the uncited mammon etymology from voice, myth and trapdoor; cut 'of all Jesus' parables' superlative and the stock line 'a fine tool and a terrible boss'.
Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 16:8 and 16:13.
Trapdoor: kyrios in 16:8 may be the master in the story or Jesus himself; commentators differ. Confirm phrasing.
Douay reads 'barrels of oil' and 'quarters of wheat' (16:6–7); the voice says 'measures of wheat'. Confirm.
Etymology of mammon ('what is trusted', from aman) is uncertain; flagged as 'perhaps' in the trapdoor.
